item.title: FINDING SISU
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Ssss… as the ladle strikes the rocks. Cedar-scented steam rises in a sudden, fragrant cloud. Heat and sweat traces down the body. Winter seems impossibly far away. Until the door opens.

Cold air rushes in. Bare feet meet the frost. Steam rising from your skin as though your entire body has begun to exhale. Somewhere ahead lies the water, dark and glacial beneath the Finnish sky. The sensible instinct is to retreat. The challenge, should you choose to accept it, may be the biggest of your life. Or at least your vacation.

Welcome to the Finnish winter, where the art of warming up has a counterpart: the exhilarating, occasionally intimidating ritual of meeting the cold. Here, sisu — that elusive Finnish quality of inner resolve, perseverance, and courage when comfort ends — takes on a new dimension. And across three very different landscapes, the water offers three ways to find it.

The journey begins with Finnair, whose newly upgraded business-class seats transform the transatlantic crossing into an opportunity to settle in and arrive refreshed. With lie-flat comfort for the overnight flight, the Finnish winter feels a little closer before the plane even touches down in Helsinki.

HELSINKI

The Urban Baltic Plunge

Helsinki wears winter beautifully. Along streets lined with ornate Art Nouveau facades, where mythical creatures and woodland motifs emerge from the stonework, Finland’s capital feels both sophisticated and quietly imaginative. At the Ateneum Art Museum, the country’s national art collection traces Finnish creativity from the 18th century through Modernism.

Afterward, head to the Old Market Hall (Vanha Kauppahalli) along the harbor. Inside this 1889 brick landmark, rich carved woodwork, narrow aisles, and cozy timber merchant stalls feel like an old-world sanctuary from the cold. Stepping up to one of the wooden counters offers a delicious introduction to local flavors—from steaming bowls of salmon soup topped with fresh dill to freshly baked rye specialties and cured Arctic fish.

For a change of scenery, board the ferry to Suomenlinna, the UNESCO World Heritage-listed sea fortress scattered across islands at the harbor entrance. Even in the depths of winter, its main paths remain clear for walking, where snow-dusted ramparts and windswept shorelines offer a dramatic view of the frozen Baltic.

As winter dusk settles over Helsinki, step into the world of Allas Sea Pool, where the Baltic meets the heart of the city. Climb down into the outdoor seawater pool and let the cold close around you, the water stretching toward the harbor while Helsinki rises behind it in a sweep of elegant waterfront buildings and glowing windows. Ferries cross the darkening sea; the last light catches the horizon before the city begins to glitter against the winter sky. The water can hover near freezing in the depths of winter, around 0–5°C (32–41°F), making the short distance from sauna to sea feel like a leap into another element entirely. Steam lifts from your skin as you surface, the skyline reflected in the rippling water, and the warm glow of the sauna beckons just steps away. At Allas, the city isn’t a view from a distant window. It surrounds you, while the Baltic itself becomes part of the experience.

Afterward, warm up high above the harbor at Palace, Helsinki’s two-Michelin-starred restaurant, where contemporary Nordic cuisine unfolds against sweeping views of the Baltic. The tasting menu draws on the region’s ingredients with precision and imagination, moving from salted whitefish with yuzu and avocado to delicate vendace roe with Lappish potato and acidulated cream, before pike perch arrives with Oscietra caviar and sweet onions. Each course offers a different expression of northern flavors, a fitting counterpoint to the bracing simplicity of the sea below.

For a luxurious retreat, The Hotel Maria offers spacious suites, a restorative spa, and a quiet sense of occasion after a day exploring the capital. Helsinki rewards those who give it time, from its Art Nouveau streets and cultural treasures to its distinctive food scene and harbor-side rituals. Helsinki does not pretend the cold is decorative. It just puts the city next to it and lets you choose.

IMATRA

Surrender on the Vuoksi River

In Finland’s Lakeland, forests gather around a vast network of lakes and waterways, and winter brings a quieter grandeur to the landscape. Near Imatra, the Vuoksi River cuts through the southeast, its flowing waters a striking counterpoint to the snow-covered banks. The region has long drawn visitors to its dramatic natural scenery, while the castle-like Imatran Valtionhotelli lends an air of old-world romance to the riverside.

Yet the most surprising way to experience this landscape is not from a scenic overlook, but from the water itself.

For dry-suit ice floating, participants slip into specially designed waterproof flotation suits before easing into the river. Warm and dry inside the suit, you lie back and float on the surface, carried gently by the current. The sensation is less a battle with the cold than a total surrender to the water: the winter sky overhead, snow-laden pine forests drifting past, and an unexpected feeling of weightlessness. Unlike a direct plunge, ice floating removes the shock of icy water while offering an intimate encounter with the river. It is an unusual expression of sisu — the willingness to trust an unfamiliar experience and let the landscape take the lead. For those seeking the classic thermal shock, traditional lakeside saunas offer the chance to step out in a swimsuit for a direct plunge into carved lake ice.

ROVANIEMI

The Arctic Lake & Celestial Sky

Beyond the Arctic Circle, winter takes on an almost otherworldly scale. At Apukka Resort, outside Rovaniemi, forests frame Lake Olkkajärvi, and the long northern nights invite travelers to look skyward. Glass-roofed igloos offer the possibility of watching for the Northern Lights from the warmth of your bed; when conditions align, their luminous green ribbons dance directly above the wilderness.

Beyond aurora gazing, the High North invites a slower immersion into the landscape. By day, visitors can trek on snowshoes through snow-heavy pine forests where deep winter silence settles over the trees, or explore local Arctic culture at the Arktikum Museum. In the evenings, private dining inside heated glass domes serves elevated Nordic cuisine surrounded by the dark forest canopy.

At the resort’s lakeside sauna, the contrast between warmth and cold becomes wonderfully immediate. Water thrown onto the hot stones releases a cloud of steam, while beyond the door Lake Olkkajärvi waits beneath the Arctic night. Apukka offers guided sauna experiences paired with a deliberate cold plunge into an ice hole cut straight into the lake. The descent down the ladder is calm and deliberate; the cold is real, and the return to the warmth of the fireside is deeply restorative. Here, sisu is less about conquering the Arctic than meeting it with curiosity, respect, and a willingness to step beyond the comfort of the known.

EDITOR’S NOTE: The author was a guest of Finnair, receiving complimentary Business Class airfare on the New York (JFK) to Helsinki route to experience their newly refurbished long-haul cabin. All opinions remain entirely independent and editorial.

item.title: A More Personal Ritual of Renewal at Meliá Chiang Mai
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Meliá Chiang Mai, wellness takes a customizable approach at YHI Spa, where a new Wellness Spa Buffet invites guests to create a treatment experience shaped around their individual needs. The concept brings together seven therapies, allowing visitors to combine traditional Thai massage, aromatic and deep tissue treatments with foot massage, body scrubs, herbal compresses, and aloe vera wraps in a two-hour spa experience. Rooted in Asian healing traditions and complemented by contemporary wellness techniques, the spa’s broader menu also includes a signature treatment that pairs Northern Thai Tok Sen techniques with Spanish massage. Seven private treatment rooms, designed around an underwater theme, provide a tranquil setting, complemented by a Thai herbal steam and sauna. Located in the heart of Chiang Mai, the spa offers travelers an opportunity to step away from the pace of exploring northern Thailand and experience a more restorative side of the city.

The Curated Take

Wellness does not always require an elaborate retreat or a complete departure from travel. Sometimes, the extraordinary is found in the opportunity to pause and choose what the body needs in that moment. Meliá Chiang Mai’s treatment concept brings an element of personal discovery to the spa experience, while its incorporation of Northern Thai healing traditions offers a connection to regional wellness practices. It is a thoughtful counterpoint to the movement and exploration that often define a journey through Chiang Mai.

item.title: When the Smokies Begin to Glow: The Extraordinary Stillness of Synchronous Fireflies
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For a brief window each June, the forests of Great Smoky Mountains National Park become the setting for one of nature’s most remarkable nighttime displays. Near Elkmont campground, thousands of synchronous fireflies illuminate the protected woodland canopy in coordinated flashes, a mating ritual that creates the rare spectacle of bioluminescence moving almost as one. Found in only a handful of places around the world, including the Smokies and Thailand, the phenomenon was little known beyond the region until the 1990s. Its growing popularity has made access to the viewing area highly limited, with a lottery system determining visitor opportunities. For travelers drawn to the natural world, the experience offers something increasingly difficult to find: a chance to witness a fleeting event that unfolds entirely on nature’s timetable, in the darkness of an ancient forest.

The Curated Take

Some of nature’s most extraordinary moments ask very little of us beyond patience and attention. The synchronous fireflies cannot be summoned or scheduled at will; they appear for a short season, on their own terms, transforming an ordinary woodland evening into something almost otherworldly. The limited viewing opportunities are part of the experience’s significance, underscoring the value of protecting natural phenomena that cannot be replicated or recreated.

item.title: Bozeman, Without the Rush: A Winter Basecamp in Montana
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Field & Stream Lodge Bozeman, the spirit of the outdoors meets the easygoing character of a Montana mountain town. The 179-room lodge, the debut property from Field & Stream Lodge Co., sits one mile from downtown Bozeman, offering a winter base for travelers who want access to the mountains without the pace and crowds of more heavily trafficked ski destinations. Bridger Bowl, a community-owned ski area just 20 minutes away, offers 2,000 acres of terrain, including its celebrated Ridge Terrain. Beyond downhill skiing, nearby Nordic trails and snowshoe routes provide quieter ways to experience the surrounding landscape, while local hot springs offer a welcome pause after a day outside. Back at the lodge, vintage-inspired Field & Stream details, wool camp blankets, canoe-shaped fire pits, and an indoor pool create a contemporary interpretation of the traditional outdoor lodge. The Dry Fly Saloon and Honey Hole add distinct gathering places, while an on-site adventure team connects guests with local guides, outfitters, rivers, and trails.

The Curated Take

Not every memorable mountain escape needs to revolve around a celebrated resort or a tightly scheduled day on the slopes. Bozeman offers another kind of winter experience, where outdoor adventure remains close at hand but the rhythm of the town is part of the appeal. Field & Stream Lodge leans into that balance, bringing the nostalgia of the American outdoor lodge into a setting where a day might lead from snow-covered trails to a neighborhood gathering place, without requiring the destination itself to become the spectacle.

item.title: The Kalinago of Dominica: A Journey Into a Living Indigenous Heritage
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At InterContinental Dominica Cabrits Resort & Spa, an excursion to the Kalinago Territory offers travelers an opportunity to encounter one of the Caribbean’s enduring Indigenous communities through its living traditions. Located along Dominica’s northeastern coast, the territory spans 3,700 acres across eight hamlets and is home to approximately 3,000 Kalinago people. Rather than approaching Indigenous heritage solely through historical accounts, the experience introduces visitors to the community’s contemporary cultural life through traditional music, dance, and storytelling, alongside generations-old artisanal practices such as basket weaving, canoe building, pottery, and wood carving. The encounter provides a window into the skills, knowledge, and customs that continue to shape Kalinago identity, offering a deeper understanding of Dominica beyond its celebrated rainforests, volcanic landscapes, and natural attractions.

The Curated Take

The most meaningful cultural encounters do more than preserve the past as something to observe. They create opportunities to recognize living communities, their knowledge, and the traditions that continue to shape their identity. The Kalinago Territory offers a perspective on Dominica that cannot be found in its scenery alone, placing the island’s Indigenous heritage and the people who carry it forward at the center of the experience.

item.title: Grenada, Beyond the Shore: The Living Traditions Behind the Island
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Six Senses La Sagesse, discovering Grenada means looking beyond its beaches to the people, landscapes, and traditions that give the island its character. A collection of locally rooted experiences invites guests into a more personal encounter with Grenadian life, beginning with Harvest Homestead, a visit to a two-acre organic farm led by Theresa Marryshow, head of Grenada’s local women’s farming organization. Guests learn about sustainable agriculture and the island’s food traditions while gaining insight into the work of local women farmers. The Hidden Haven excursion pairs a journey to the Seven Sisters Waterfalls with wellness and culinary elements, while the Reggae Fields Journey introduces guests to Grenadian cocoa farmers and beekeepers before inviting them to make their own cocoa balls. Together, these experiences reveal an island whose richness is found not only in its natural beauty, but in the knowledge, livelihoods, and cultural practices sustained by its communities.

The Curated Take

There is a particular depth to travel that makes room for the people who know a place best. On Grenada, a farm visit, a conversation with a beekeeper, or the making of a traditional cocoa treat can offer a more lasting connection than simply passing through a beautiful landscape. These encounters give the island’s natural appeal a human dimension, revealing the quiet richness of traditions carried forward through everyday life.

item.title: A Winter Worth Lingering For: Alpine Indulgence at Bachelor Gulch
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At The Ritz-Carlton, Bachelor Gulch, winter in Colorado’s Beaver Creek mountains extends well beyond the ski slopes. The 2026/27 season brings together alpine adventure, culinary discovery, restorative wellness, and festive traditions in a setting designed for both exhilaration and lingering fireside moments. Ski-in, ski-out access to Beaver Creek Mountain provides a natural starting point, while new experiences invite guests to explore another side of mountain life: a hands-on Cocktail Atelier with the resort’s lead mixologists, a guided Dom Pérignon and caviar tasting, and a private raclette dinner at historic Anderson Cabin. The resort’s 21,000-square-foot spa offers another kind of winter retreat, with therapeutic treatments, sound healing, red-light LED therapy, and restorative facilities. Beyond the slopes, guided snowshoe excursions and hands-on Art in Nature workshops offer opportunities to engage with the landscape at a gentler pace. Seasonal celebrations add to the atmosphere, from the annual tree lighting and holiday programming to Hanukkah observances and New Year’s Eve dining.

The Curated Take

The appeal of a mountain escape is not always measured in vertical feet or hours spent on the slopes. At Bachelor Gulch, the winter experience is shaped by the contrast between outdoor adventure and the pleasures of staying in: a private alpine dinner, a carefully guided tasting, or an evening gathered around a three-story stone fireplace. That balance gives the destination a broader appeal, making it as inviting for travelers drawn to the rituals of winter as for those who come specifically to ski.

item.title: Mui Ne Takes to the Wind: A Coastal Adventure at The Anam
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
From November through March, the Northeast Monsoon transforms Mui Ne, Vietnam, into a spectacular setting for kitesurfing, with colorful sails filling the skies above its coastline. The Anam Mui Ne is introducing a seasonal experience that brings guests closer to this distinctive coastal culture through its Windswept Adrenaline Tour. The half-day excursion begins with a private Jeep safari along the shore, continuing to Hon Rom Beach for views of the kitesurfers before a private introductory workshop at Ca Ty Beach, where certified instructors demonstrate the fundamentals of kite control on land. An expert freestyle performance follows, offering a closer look at the sport’s skill and spectacle. The afternoon concludes with a private sunset picnic by the sea. Designed for beginners as well as curious observers, the experience offers a fresh way to discover the winds, scenery, and outdoor culture that have made Mui Ne one of Asia’s leading kitesurfing destinations.

The Curated Take

Some destinations are defined by a particular relationship with the elements. In Mui Ne, the seasonal winds are more than a feature of the weather; they have shaped the coastline’s identity and drawn an international community of kitesurfers. The Anam’s experience offers an accessible introduction to that local character, balancing the energy of the sport with the quieter pleasure of watching the sails move across the water as daylight fades. It is a reminder that a memorable resort experience can begin by looking beyond the property and discovering what makes its surroundings distinctive.

item.title: “Stars Align”: Los Angeles Unveils the Slogan for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
As Los Angeles prepares to welcome the world for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, LA28 has unveiled “Stars Align” as the official slogan for the event, capturing the meeting of athletic achievement, collective ambition, and the creative energy of its host city. Introduced through a global campaign film set to the Red Hot Chili Peppers’ “Can’t Stop,” the slogan draws on the idea that extraordinary moments emerge when years of dedication meet a defining opportunity. The film brings together iconic Los Angeles landmarks, including the Hollywood Sign and Griffith Observatory, with the city’s golden-hour light, diverse communities, and memorable moments from the history of the Games. The Olympic Opening Ceremony is scheduled for July 14, 2028, followed by the Paralympic Opening Ceremony on August 15. Los Angeles will become the third city to host the Summer Olympics three times and will welcome its first-ever Paralympic Games.

The Curated Take

A host city does more than provide venues for the Olympic Games. It becomes part of the story, shaping the atmosphere, cultural encounters, and memories that stay with visitors long after the final competition. “Stars Align” places Los Angeles’s identity as a city of imagination and possibility at the center of that story. With its blend of sporting history, entertainment, distinctive neighborhoods, and Southern California landscapes, the 2028 Games offer an opportunity to experience the city through a global celebration that extends well beyond the stadium.

item.title: Hollywood Storytelling Takes Center Stage at the LA28 Olympic Games
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles are bringing together two defining expressions of the city’s global identity: sport and entertainment. LA28 has appointed acclaimed film producer Kathleen Kennedy as Head of Ceremonies and Content, where she will lead the development and delivery of all four Opening and Closing Ceremonies. An eight-time Academy Award nominee and former president of Lucasfilm, Kennedy has helped shape some of cinema’s most recognizable films and franchises, with more than 70 feature film credits. She joins Executive Producer Peter Rice, Creative Director Ben Winston, and veteran ceremonies producer Scott Givens as preparations move toward production. The Olympic Opening Ceremony is scheduled for July 14, 2028, with the Paralympic Games following in August. Across iconic Los Angeles venues, including the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the ceremonies will draw on the city’s creative influence to introduce the Games to a global audience.

The Curated Take

Major sporting events offer a rare opportunity for a destination to tell its story on a truly global stage. For Los Angeles, that story naturally extends beyond the competition itself, drawing on a cultural identity shaped by film, music, entertainment, and an enduring ability to create spectacle. Kennedy’s appointment brings considerable storytelling experience to that ambition. The ceremonies will be an important part of how visitors and billions of viewers encounter Los Angeles in 2028, positioning the city not simply as a host, but as part of the experience.
